utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, ma'am. I welcome, everybody. And good morning, everybody. I notice the absence of accused Pandurevic. We have already received the waiver, so Mr. Sarapa, I take it we can proceed. Representation. Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Elderkin for the Prosecution. Absent from the Defence teams, I notice Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Krgovic, Mr. Haynes. Before we start, a motion for protected measures for the witness was filed yesterday evening, I take it. Are you all aware of it? Because it was filed at a late hour. Yes, you are. Are there any objections? Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No objections from our side, but I'd just like to introduce our new legal assistant, Ms. Negosava Smiljanic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm glad to see that you and other Defence teams are taking on board additional staff now, as we approach a critical moment. I think it's very useful. Welcome, madam. Any objections to the granting of protective measures. We hear none. Motion granted. So this guy will have face and voice distortion, plus pseudonym. Otherwise, the hearing will be in public session, except of course for the critical parts, like his identity and so on. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The pseudonym being ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 175, it should be, yes. It should be 175. Okay. Can we bring in the witness. We keep the curtains down until he comes in, and then we'll put them up again. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he will need a caution, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to welcome you. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you are required by our Rules to enter a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. You are being handed the text now. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. As I said, you are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, however, there are a couple of things. You can start pulling the curtains up again, please. Before you start giving evidence, however, I would like to inform you of the following: First, that upon your request, the Prosecution asked for some protective measures to be put in place to protect your identity. We asked the various Defence teams this morning if they had any objection to such protective measures, and they have all agreed that we should grant the protective measures, or, rather, they have not objected to the granting, so we have put in place the following protective measures: Pseudonym, in other words, you will be referred to not by your name, but by a number; and then facial and voice distortion. I take it the nature of these measures have already been explained to you before coming into this courtroom. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are satisfied with this arrangement, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then there is another thing that I need to inform you about, and that's in the form of an advisory, and I suggest you pay careful attention to what I'm going to tell you now. There may be questions put to you -- I'm not saying that there will, but there may be questions put to you, which if you answer truthfully, could possibly expose you to criminal proceedings; in other words, could incriminate you. You would be incriminating yourself. In such a case, our Rules provide for a remedy in the form of a right which you have to ask the Trial Chamber to exempt you from answering such questions. This is not, however, an absolute rule, in the sense that we can grant such exemption, but we can also refuse it after hearing what you have to say. If we grant the exemption, then obviously you don't answer the question. If we order you to answer such questions, then the privilege that you have is in the form of an additional right; namely, that whatever you say which is self-incriminatory will then not be capable of being used against you. In other words, if you say things that could expose you to criminal proceedings, if there are criminal proceedings, whatever you would have said would not be used in those proceedings, cannot be used in those proceedings. Was this explained to you before you came into the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you fully understand the extent of its import?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So having said that, I think we can proceed. Mr. McCloskey will lead, will have some questions for you. I assume he will then be followed by some of the Defence teams, if at all. Mr. McCloskey, you still expect one hour or, sorry, 75 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. First of all, I'm going to show you a sheet of paper. It's our number 65 ter 4459, and can you tell us if this is your name. We don't want it out loud, but we just want to confirm your identity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could go into private session for just a moment, a few initial questions, and then we'll go into open. And so my questions now, sir, no one will hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment until we get to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it true that you have, in questioning by the Office of the Prosecutor, been shown a vehicle log for a minivan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I don't remember the picture, but I was shown a vehicle log.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did that -- looking at that vehicle log, did that help remind you of a trip you took on July 23rd, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell the Court, as best as you can remember, about that trip? Who first told you you were going -- you had a specific task that day on the 23rd of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: That specific task, if I remember, there were two rides. I'm not exactly sure, but I was issued this task by my commander, the commander of the administrative headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And give us his name, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Momo Amovic. That's what they called him. I don't know if he goes by another name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were issued a task by Momo Amovic on the 23rd of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, please, sir, when you know -- when you know something, just tell us. When you're not sure, please tell us as well, but please don't preface everything with you're not sure, unless that's absolutely true. Now, tell us, what did Mr. Amovic tell you to do that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, I had a previous trip to do, and when I came back outside the administrative headquarters, he told me to drive some people who were there by the road at that place indicated on the log. I went and did as I had been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So where did you go to get these people you referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Somewhere down towards Tesca [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you mention another little village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Dragasevac Tesca. That's on the same road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you go in this Dragasevac area? Pardon me for the pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Dragasevac. I went there, and he told me to take them to the battalion. I didn't ask why or how. I was not entitled to put questions. I turned around and went to execute the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: Where did you go in Dragasevac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I went from Vlasenica to Dragasevac. They were by the road over there. I took them inside and drove them to Bisina, to Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there any buildings by the road where you picked them up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Some houses in rubble, destroyed. I didn't look carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that a unit of men that were living in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were living there or not. I did not notice any civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you've described that as a special unit to us. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I don't know if it was a unit or if those were some particular people. I had never seen them there, and I had never taken such people for a ride.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall earlier describing the different ethnic make-up of those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I heard them talking. One of them or two or three of them were Muslims, and there were a couple of Croats, as far as I could judge from their conversation. I did not know them, so I can't tell you anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many of them got into your vehicle that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Five or six. I did not count, because the first one who got in started to insult me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: They were masked, with caps over their heads, some fingerless gloves, and they had overalls of different colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they have any military appearance, or were these mechanics' overalls or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, like military fatigues, but they were all different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were any of them armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: The first two had weapons, but as far as the others are concerned, I did not dare look at them, so I couldn't see. But I could see the first two were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why would you not dare look at, you know, six soldiers that you picked up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, because the first one who got on broke the mirror with his rifle, and he suggested, Look ahead. And after that, I didn't dare turn around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what vehicle were you driving that day that they got into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: The minibus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was anyone else with you, besides these men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you then drive to the place you were told to take them by your commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: At first, the commander told me to go to the brigade, but then we changed direction, and I don't know whether it was the 3rd or the 4th Battalion because I never asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all, what brigade are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: We are talking about, I suppose, the Sekovici Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I think you would know the brigade, so let me ask you again. What brigade are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, I don't know which battalion of theirs was up there because I never inquired whether it was the 4th, the 5th, the 3rd. I have no idea which one it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you -- don't worry about the battalions at this point. I'm just -- the brigade we are talking about, what brigade area was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Supposedly the Sekovic Brigade. How can I know? The Sekovic Brigade, presumably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you mentioned, I belive, and I don't think the interpreters didn't pick it up, but a place where you were told to go. Where were you told to go by your commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I was to drive them to the battalion, the Sekovic Brigada, Brigade, since they changed the plan and they sent us directly to the battalion where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: In Bisina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "they changed the plan," who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: One of the men who boarded the bus, when we were approaching Sekovici, he just told me, Drive to Pasina, or Bisina. I don't know who had told him. I then I complied, I just made a detour and drove towards Pasina -- Bisina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We need to get this right. Can you -- and it's just a little trouble with the translation. What is the name of the area where you went, Pasina or Bisina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: You know what, I think it's Bisina. I'm not a surveyor to give you the exact names, but I know it's called Bisina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time of day was this when you were driving this group to Bisina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Sometime around noon. I cannot remember exactly, but I think it's recorded in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll go over the log-book briefly near the end. I just want to have you tell this before we get to that. Now, where precisely did you drive to? Can you describe to the area where you stopped the car, the minivan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: It was somewhere close to their HQ, some 200 or 300 metres, I cannot tell you exactly, from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was it along the main asphalt road or somewhere else that you stopped the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: No, it's up there. It's a macadam road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what was around the place where you stopped the minivan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Along the way, I saw a building being built. On the right-hand side, there was water, and maybe a kilometre or two ahead I stopped. There was a man there, an elderly man. He didn't have all his teeth, and his clothes were rather shabby. He stopped us. They all alighted. He told me to turn around and wait over there where they were building this barracks and where this water was. They got out. I turned around and went back, while they proceeded along the road towards the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Besides this old person with missing teeth, did you see anybody else in that area when you pulled up your minivan there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I saw another two or three civilians who were minding the cattle or were picking raspberries. I don't know exactly what they were doing. Because there was a forest, I wasn't able to see much more. I think I saw a couple of persons there. Whether they were security or not, I don't know because I didn't go closer. And I also saw two vehicles parked in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of vehicles did you see parked in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: As far as I remember, one -- one 110 vehicle and one Pinzgauer, or maybe an ambulance vehicle. I'm not sure, but I saw these two vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you say a 110 vehicle, can you tell us the -- what the brand name that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: That's a TAM-110 truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the Pinzgauer, what kind of a vehicle was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, it's a vehicle for various purposes. It's an all-terrain vehicle. I never drove one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when these men that you brought over in the minivan got out of the minivan, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: With what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: They had rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I suppose automatic ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And tell us what happened as you waited there, after they left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, I went back for about one kilometre. I don't remember if I went anywhere. There was some people building some house there, but I don't know what they were doing. I never approached them or asked them what they were doing. I just had some water to drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've told us, in the interview, about seeing some men with belts, and you described the colour of the belt. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: While I was standing there and they were getting out, I noticed, close to the command, three or four men in uniform. Whether it was their army posted there to secure the command headquarters or not, I don't know, because I never went near them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about the belts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, they had yellow belts, maybe white. I don't remember precisely because I -- I couldn't see much. They were far away. I just saw these men standing there, but what they were doing, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did those men that you drove in the minibus come back to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: When do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That day, after you dropped them off, did you have to take them back home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes. Since the commander told me at the beginning that the front-line had been broken through, I was told to wait for them and take them back, and I did what I had been told to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How long was it before they came back? How long did you wait until they showed up again at your minivan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you precisely. If I remember, it lasted three, four, five hours. I don't know exactly, but this can also be found in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What were they doing, as far as you know, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know, because my commander told me that the line had been breached and that I had to drive them to the 4th Battalion. However, what they did there, I -- I have no idea. I wasn't there with them. I was waiting for them in the vicinity of the builders, so I cannot give you any precise data. I'm reluctant to tell you something that would be untrue; therefore, I don't know what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you still scared of these men, like you were when they got on your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Because I had troubles with them before, and some other people, who persecuted me because I had been in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When they came back, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I was standing next to the vehicle. Suddenly, I heard someone's voice. A man was with me who was watering his cattle, and I suddenly noticed them coming and walking towards me. I got on the minibus. They also got on in the minibus. They went and took seats behind and told me to drive them to the spot where I had picked them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was it that you were dropping them off to? I mean, surely not just in the middle of the road somewhere.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I took them to the exact place where they got on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at the vehicle log that you've seen before. It's P04432, and, sir, that will come up on your screen. I have the original, too, which I'll show in a minute, but let's have you work with the screen for a minute, since everyone else is looking at that as well. If we could put the first page of the B/C/S on that. It shouldn't be broadcast. If we could blow up the right side. The left side really isn't important for my questioning. Okay. Sir, first of all, can you tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I need my glasses, and it's in my jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your jacket's in the witness room?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Could someone --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the inside pocket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll bring it over to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, if you need to take a break for any reason, you know, just let me know, and you can take a break.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. While we're waiting for your glasses, can you tell us what the vehicle work log is? We'll go over the details when you can see it, but can you tell us, just generally, what it's used for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: The vehicle work log is a sheet which serves for recording the use of a vehicle, including all the data relating to the fuel, the lubricants, and other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you had told us that your supervisors were a bit worried about you because you'd gone to Serbia at once in your career, you'd gone AWOL; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You told us that your supervisors were a bit worried about you, kind of looking at you closely, because at one point you had gone to Serbia without permission; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: What do you mean? During the war or -- I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, during the war. You went to Serbia without permission, right, and you got in trouble with your supervisors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was it your job to fill in this report for this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I wasn't supposed to sign it. I was only supposed to record the journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you record the journey accurately when you were recording and filling this out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Whatever's written in my handwriting, I can vouch, say that it's true. But as for the others, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at this first page, and I'm going to give you the original so you can see the original just of the first page now. Now, we can all see that this says "minibus." Is that the minibus you drove on that day, on the 23rd of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now I notice -- I notice you're looking on the back page, and we'll get to the back page, but could you flip over and look at the first page so we can talk about that for a minute. And do you see your name on that first page as one of the drivers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you see your handwriting anywhere on that first page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to the second page. Now, before we blow it up, do you see your handwriting on this page anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe where you see your handwriting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: You can find it in -- under the item dated 19th of July, also 20th of July and 21st of July, and 23rd of July as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the 24th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: No, that's -- it's one of my colleagues' handwriting for the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So as we look on this document from the 19th to the 23rd, we see several columns at the top, and it goes "1" through "20." You have told us before that all of those columns were your handwriting, except column 20; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I can see here from the 19th, so my handwriting is for the 19th and the 23rd. The 24th was not, because I was driving a different vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's go directly to the 23rd, where we see it says "Vlasenica-Sekovici-Bisina-Sekovici." Is that the trip that you've described today in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that your handwriting, having written "Vlasenica-Sekovici-Bisina-Sekovici"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And under the total people carried, number 8, did you write that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was -- it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so does that eight include you, or is that only the people -- the number of people you carried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Including me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So then we get to column 10, and it says "Kilometres: 48." Is that roughly accurate for the trip you took?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, more or less, it's correct, because tachograph was inoperable, and the commander took these distances from the map and told me to record them as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then we go to the sections where people's names are handwritten in. I want to -- it looks like 16, 17, 18, 19, and what's the name of the person that's handwritten in there for the 23rd of July, the first one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: 23rd of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Are you referring to the first name that we can see, 16, 17, and 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: It's written here "Popovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does it say "Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Whether he was a lieutenant-colonel or colonel, I don't know which rank he had. It just says here "Popovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we blow that up, section -- July 23rd, section 16, 17, and 18 over on the far right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we can see something before "Popovic" on this, can't we? It's an abbreviation, it looks like to me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: It reads -- yes, I see, it says "PUK." This is probably it, "P. PUK Popovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's your handwriting; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you wrote that down there; correct? Or did you write that down there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I wrote this down because after I finished this and the log wasn't signed on the spot, I asked who's going to sign this. He told me, Leave it on the desk and get out. And that is what I did. When I came back after two or three days, the same happened. My boss, who was in charge of material and finances, he asked me whose signature this is. I told him that I left the sheet with my boss and that I also cannot discern whose signature this was. He asked what was happening. I found this signature to be very suspicious, because I didn't sign it; I just filled in and left the room. And the same happened with all the other items that were initially without the signature and were later given a signature. So you can see my signature earlier, but whose signatures came later on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, are you saying you filled in the name "Popovic" after it was signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes, yes, as far as I can remember, particularly these journeys. You can also see that my colleague filled it out afterwards. When we finished the journey, the person who used the car should sign it on the spot. Since this gentleman who was supposed to sign it for the trip where I took these gentlemen wasn't around, I asked my boss what to do. So even without a signature, I had to indicate the journey that I took. Now, who signed this, I don't know. I found it suspicious, so I had to make some mark on it. You can see also, from the subsequent entries, that the signatures were put at a later date. I had troubles on a couple of occasions that they wanted to send me back on the front. That is why I recorded everything accurately, in the event of any of my officers inquired about what I was doing, but I don't know who signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you did write down "Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic" three times, as it's indicated in this record; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, every time when I went on a trip, that's what I would do. If the user of the services is not there during the trip, I bring the log to my boss, I bring back the keys, and I go back to my dorm. Or if I am going home and the vehicle is needed, another driver gets in and takes it. I don't know exactly how the gentleman signs, whether it's really his signature or not. I cannot comment upon that. But I asked the boss of the assets and finances service immediately. I left the log-book with him and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you -- you printed Popovic's name in this log-book; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: I did write it in block letters when the man asked me about the signature. He asked me, Where did you go? Who was in charge? And I said, Popovic, I wrote down "Popovic," because that's what I had been told. The man did not sign the log. I normally don't leave the car until my log-book is signed, because I know I will get in trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, so you just said: "I did write in block letters, which the man asked me about the signature. He asked me, Where did you go? Who was in charge? And I said, Popovic, I wrote down 'Popovic,' because that's what I had been told. The man did not sign the log. I normally don't leave the car until my log-book is signed, because I know I will get in trouble." So you stand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, but I also added something about the signature, because this was not signed immediately. I didn't even see the man there, and that's what I emphasised. The same happened with those entries where it said -- where it says "Drago." I had to put it in there as an approximation. Somebody from their service was in charge. I couldn't go into that. I just carried out the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Somebody from whose service was in charge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, that service, you know, the service that the boss indicated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tell us. I mean, we know there's different services in the army, but what service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, the security service. I don't know what to call it. I'm not a very literate man, and I don't know much about the distribution of services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, why did you think Popovic was in charge, to have written that on this log-book like you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, because my boss said, well, probably Popovic. I could not argue with him. I wrote what he said; I left the paper on his desk. And where he carried the log from there on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, did your boss say "probably Popovic," or did he say "Popovic"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: He said, Probably Popovic. It was a long time ago, but as far as I remember, he said, Well, Popovic, I suppose. I really don't know whether it was him or someone else from his service. I don't make these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you briefly about the entry on the 19th. We have an intercept where the Prosecution believes is a mention of a Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic having some job he's doing on the 19th, distributing something, I believe. What can you tell us about what you were doing on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, if I remember correctly, it says here something about the 19th, and I -- it's probably as I described it earlier. I went to Vlasenica, Tesca and Jakovica; that's some village where the battalion was. I don't know exactly what it was about. Perhaps those people were on leave, so the soldiers from Vlasenica went there. I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to draw your attention to, and we can see it right at the top of the page -- we know the first two lines are from the 19th. We see the first line says "Colonel Popovic," and the second line is "Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic," and that's your handwriting, isn't it, that you wrote that in there too; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is my signature -- it's my handwriting, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were working with Colonel Popovic that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't even see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So why did you write his name down there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Well, because some job was being done for his service or involving his people, the trip to Jakovica and the driving back to Sekovici. In those days, I didn't see much of him; maybe once during a lineup, but I didn't really look carefully, and I didn't have any contact with him because I practically didn't know him. I did not go upstairs, as a rule. It was out of bounds for me. During those days, I didn't see him at all, I believe. I saw him perhaps that once during a lineup. I was just a regular soldier. I did not normally speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, it's the position of the Prosecution, and I'm very glad that you came to testify today, but that you know much more than you're telling. You know that people were executed at Bisina, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-175
utterances.text: Let me tell you very honestly. After all the torture they inflicted upon me, I am very bitter. If I knew anything else, I would certainly tell you, but since I don't know anything but what I could read from the media -- and for every of these trips, I wouldn't have let him off if he had been there. He would have had to sign for himself. Everyone who uses a vehicle is obliged to sign for it. Really, for this day, the 19th, somebody from that service, from their service, perhaps issued an order to my boss, saying, Drive these people to Jakovci, to that battalion. They must return to their position, and that was it. Apart from that, I couldn't say anything, because I really don't know what was going on. I mean, whatever I said would be perhaps untrue, and, I mean, I don't remember anything else happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like just briefly to consult my client; very, very briefly, for a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course. The security guards, please make that possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic. Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have questions, Judge Kwon, Judge Stole? Sir, you will be pleased to know that we don't require your presence any further, because your testimony comes to an end here. You're free to go, and you will receive assistance from our staff to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony, and I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anything else before we adjourn? Yes, the pseudonym sheet and the log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are already in evidence. I don't need to ask if there is any objection to the tendering of the pseudonym sheet? It's admitted and to be kept under seal, please. Anything else? None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. So to revert to the public aspect of it, so by Friday we expect a further motion from you. We are to expect a further motion for further reopening and further rebuttal. Thank you. We stand adjourned now. You will soon know, because we will be -- I actually have already signed it, but we'll be issuing orders as regards scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.18 a.m.
